title: The tyranny of the progression statement
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou asks why vague progression statements such as I can infer characters emotions from explicit details in the text persist decades after England abolished national curriculum levels, and why they are common across Scotland, Wales, the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Her diagnosis is that they follow logically from the belief that skills like inference can be taught directly, when in fact inference depends on vocabulary, background knowledge and text complexity. They also survive because critics rarely offer a workable alternative, and replacing them forces precision about the curriculum itself. She cites Christine Counsell's test of reordering history statements and Christopher Such's examples to show the statements cannot discriminate between year groups. Her practical proposal is to back each statement with a set of closed questions, which exposes what is meant and reveals weak curriculum design. The piece ends with a pointer to No More Marking's own Writing Progression quiz sequence.
points: Progression statements stay popular because they are the logical outcome of treating skills such as inference as discrete and directly teachable.
Counsell's exercise of reordering ten history statements, which nobody could do accurately, shows how little information the wording carries.
Replacing statements is hard because greater specificity forces a specific, shareable curriculum, which is much harder to adopt than a spreadsheet of statements.
Backing each statement with ten or so closed questions forces schools to decide what they actually mean at that point in the curriculum.
Assessment operationalises curriculum, so writing questions will expose a weak curriculum rather than hide it.
quotes: The problem with these statements is that they are too vague and imprecise to provide useful information for a teacher or student, as you can see below.

She would take a set of ten progression statements in history that were meant to run from year 1 to year 11. Then she would ask people to put them back together in the right order. No-one could do it accurately, because they were just word salad.

If you think that inference is a discrete skill, then a statement like “can infer insightfully” makes sense. Once you realise that inference is not a discrete skill, and that your ability to infer depends on vocabulary, background knowledge and text complexity, then you realise why these systems don’t work.
But it is not easy to change to a new, better system precisely because these statements go beyond mere assessment and have huge implications for the curriculum & pedagogy.
Setting these questions would force you to think about exactly what you mean by this statement at this particular point in the curriculum.

If you have a good curriculum, this process should be relatively straightforward. If you don’t have a good curriculum, this process will probably expose that. As Dylan Wiliam says, “assessment operationalises curriculum”.
Backing up statements with questions grounds them in specificity and reality and creates a genuinely common language – not just the illusion of one.
